newsitem.title: SUDAN: Sudan signs peace deal with some southern rebels.
newsitem.headline: Sudan signs peace deal with some southern rebels.

text.p: Sudan and a group of former rebel factions on Monday signed a peace deal which Khartoum hopes will help end a 14-year guerrilla war raging in the south.

But the five factions which signed the deal in Khartoum do not include the Sudan People's Liberation Army (SPLA) of John Garang, the largest group which does most of the fighting against the government and has vowed to continue.
The opposition in exile said this made the deal meaningless.
But Sudan's cabinet this month said: "It meets demands that led to the eruption of the war in the south and guarantees political, economic and social rights for all citizens."

A Sudan government statement on Monday said the agreement allows division of powers and wealth between the federal and state governments, and says Islamic sharia is the main source of law but states may enact laws which complement it.
It says it prohibits discrimination, guarantees freedoms, and sees an interim period to rehabilitate the south, set up a democratic system and start a self-determination referendum.

"The agreement provides for self-determination to be conducted after four years in which citizens of the southern region who would compose the voting force would be given free will to choose between unity or separation," it said.

Exiled opposition leaders said the deal was virtually meaningless because Garang's SPLA was not a party and that it was bound to fail to end the war because it was signed by allies of the government. They saw its shortcomings as not allowing for the birth of a democratic, multi-party system.
"We look at it as a fake trial to try and break the splendid isolation the regime is living in," National Democratic Alliance (NDA) spokesman Farouq Abu Eissa told Reuters in Cairo.
The NDA is the umbrella opposition organisation which includes the SPLA and other rebel groups which since January have stepped up a campaign to topple the Islamist government.
"Such a regime based on fundamentalist ideals can never produce anything of a 'multi' nature," said Eissa.
Sudan has been riven by civil war since 1983, with the mainly Christian and animist south fighting what it sees as domination by the Moslem Arabised north.

Gabriel Mathiang, speaking in Cairo for the SPLA's political wing, said: "The people who are signing the charter with Khartoum are friends. How can you sign a charter with your friends? They have come to sign a charter with their own stooges. It is actually not going to work because they don't control the ground."
The groups which signed are splinter factions with few fighters, mostly fighting the SPLA as pro-government militias.

The deal finalises an April 1996 charter Khartoum signed with faction leaders Kerubino Kwanyin Bol of the Sudan People's Liberation Army-Bahr al-Ghazal and Riak Machar of Southern Sudan Independence Movement (SSIM).

Other factions later joined Khartoum's peace initiative and on Monday the Equatoria Defence Force, the Independence Kawaz Makwei and the Independence of Bor factions also signed with Sudan's First Vice President Lt-Gen Al-Zubeir Mohammad Saleh.
A former political opposition group, the Union of Sudan African Parties, also signed the agreement and SPLA-Nuba faction signed separate deals with the government.
SPLA spokesman Sampson Kwaje called the main deal a "sham".

"You will notice it is being signed as we are stepping up our offensive. Khartoum is planning these factions will now be told they have to fight the SPLA to protect their government in the south," he told Reuters in Nairobi.
Former U.S. president Jimmy Carter was quoted on Sunday in Sudan as saying he and President Omar Hassan al-Bashir discussed the possibility of expanding the peace deal to other parties.

Carter left the capital for the southern rebel-held town of Yei to meet Garang, U.S. officials said. But in Nairobi, a rebel spokesman said on Monday a government warplane bombed Yei on Sunday, preventing Carter from landing to meet Garang.
